DETROIT, Michigan (CNN) -- It's a stimulus plan on sneakers. The NCAA men's Final Four at Detroit's Ford Field could generate $30 million to $50 million from visitors. The NCAA men's basketball Final Four couldn't come at a better time for the city of Detroit -- the hard-hit capital of the U.S. auto industry at the center of the state of Michigan's economic woes. The 12-percent unemployment rate here is the highest in the nation, and with the Big Three automakers all needing multibillion-dollar government bailouts in an attempt to stay afloat, the future isn't much brighter, some say. "We need some help," said Detroit resident Mark Franklin, who took his 5-year-old son to Friday's Hershey's College All-Star Game at Ford Field. "There are too many people out of work already. Even if you have a job, you know someone who doesn't." Enter the Final Four and a quartet of powerhouse college basketball teams -- all seeking NCAA brass. Connecticut, Michigan State, North Carolina and Villanova have won a combined nine NCAA championships and reached 31 Final Fours. But more important to the city are the visitors -- and the wallets -- that college basketball's marquee weekend will bring to Detroit. City leaders expect 100,000 fans to visit -- staying in hotel rooms, renting cars and spending an anticipated $30 million to $50 million. The participation of Michigan State adds icing on the cake. The school's campus sits just 90 miles away, in East Lansing, giving the Spartans a home-floor advantage as they give locals some added pride on a special weekend. MSU helped things along mightily by advancing to the finals Saturday, defeating Connecticut 82-73. In the national championship game, the Spartans will play North Carolina, 83-69 victors over Villanova later Saturday. More than half the Michigan State players are from in-state and many have felt the impact of the region's economic woes. "I have family that are unemployed right now," said sophomore guard Durrell Summers, who starred at Detroit's Redford Covenant High School. "[For the Final Four] to bring that kind of money in, hopefully it can help open up jobs for my family and for other families because some people got laid off for no reason." Watch Elaine Quijano's report on a GM dealer's perspective . Detroit's first Final Four is the latest in a series of big sporting events for the city. The Pistons have hosted a pair of NBA Finals in suburban Auburn Hills, while the NHL's Red Wings have won two Stanley Cups at downtown Joe Louis Arena. Baseball's Tigers have played in a World Series and its home, Comerica Park, hosted an MLB All-Star game. This weekend's host venue, Ford Field, was the site of Super Bowl XL and Oakland Hills Country Club was home to the 2004 Ryder Cup and the PGA Championship last August in nearby Bloomfield Hills. This is the first year of a new stadium configuration for the Final Four, requiring host domes to use all permanent seating to meet a 70,000-seat minimum. "You see people driving up just to take a picture of the Final Four sign on (Ford Field). It's something to be proud of," Franklin said. "Now we need city leaders to take advantage of it."

## The 2009 Final Four: a short-lived economic lift for crisis-era Detroit

When Detroit hosted the NCAA men’s Final Four at Ford Field on April 4–6, 2009, the event arrived at an unusually bleak moment. General Motors and Chrysler were surviving on federal assistance—Chrysler would enter bankruptcy later that month and GM in June—while Michigan’s unemployment rate was about 12.6%, the highest in the country. Detroit itself was contending with severe job losses, foreclosures and falling tax revenue.

Against that backdrop, the Final Four provided both a burst of visitor spending and a rare positive national spotlight.

### Scale and immediate impact

Local organizers and the Detroit Metro Convention & Visitors Bureau projected roughly **$30 million in direct visitor spending** and an overall regional impact commonly estimated at **$50 million to $52 million**. The money flowed principally to:

- Downtown and suburban hotels  
- Restaurants, bars and entertainment venues  
- Parking operators and transportation companies  
- Caterers, security firms and temporary-event workers  
- Local attractions and retail businesses  

Ford Field drew announced crowds of **72,456 for the semifinals** and **72,922 for the championship game**, the latter then an NCAA title-game attendance record. Michigan State’s participation was especially valuable because it brought tens of thousands of additional fans from elsewhere in the state while keeping the event’s local interest high through Monday night.

Hotels in and around downtown reported heavy bookings, and restaurants near Ford Field, Greektown and Campus Martius experienced one of their busiest weekends of the recession.

### What residents said

For many Detroiters, the benefit was as psychological as it was financial. Contemporary local and national reports repeatedly captured residents describing the tournament as a needed reprieve. Typical comments included:

> “This is what Detroit needs right now.”

and:

> “It’s a breath of fresh air.”

Residents and downtown workers pointed to crowded sidewalks, full restaurants and favorable television images as evidence that Detroit could still stage a major national event. Others were more cautious, noting that a three-day sports festival could not replace lost manufacturing jobs or repair the city’s finances.

That distinction is important: the widely cited $50-million figure was a **gross economic-impact estimate**, not new government revenue or long-term economic growth. Some spending merely shifted from other local activities, and part of the income went to national hotel chains, the NCAA and companies based outside Detroit.

### Michigan State’s “play for the state” message

Michigan State’s run to the championship game intensified the event’s meaning. The Spartans defeated Connecticut in the national semifinal before losing to North Carolina, 89–72, in the final.

Players openly connected their tournament run to the economic hardships facing Michigan. Guard **Kalin Lucas** said:

> “Everybody’s losing jobs. The economy is bad. We just want to give them something to smile about.”

Forward **Draymond Green**, a freshman at the time, emphasized that the team represented more than the university:

> “We’re not only playing for Michigan State. We’re playing for the whole state of Michigan.”

Detroit native **Durrell Summers** similarly described the run as larger than basketball:

> “It’s bigger than us. It’s bigger than Michigan State. It’s for the whole state of Michigan.”

Their comments became part of the weekend’s central narrative: a team from the state capital playing in Detroit on behalf of communities battered by layoffs and uncertainty.

### Longer-term significance

The Final Four did not materially reverse Detroit’s economic decline. Its spending was temporary, most jobs associated with it were short-term, and the auto bankruptcies soon overwhelmed the tournament in economic importance.

Nevertheless, it produced several real gains:

1. **A concentrated infusion of visitor spending** during a deep recession.  
2. **National exposure for downtown Detroit** and Ford Field as major-event venues.  
3. **Higher morale and civic visibility** at a moment when coverage of Detroit was dominated by industrial collapse.  
4. **Evidence that the city could successfully host very large events**, building on Super Bowl XL in 2006 and supporting later convention and sports bids.

The fairest conclusion is that the 2009 Final Four was not an economic rescue plan. It was a successful, highly visible weekend that delivered tens of millions of dollars in estimated activity and a temporary emotional lift—valuable precisely because Detroit’s underlying crisis was so severe.

**Principal contemporary reference points:** NCAA attendance records; Detroit Metro Convention & Visitors Bureau impact projections; March 2009 Bureau of Labor Statistics unemployment data; and April 2009 reporting by the Associated Press, *Detroit Free Press*, *The Detroit News*, ESPN and other tournament media.

**Michigan State, North Carolina advance to title game as Final Four energizes Detroit**

**DETROIT —** Michigan State turned its home-state Final Four into a celebration Saturday night, defeating Connecticut 82-73 before a roaring crowd at Ford Field and advancing to the national championship game for the first time since 2000.

The Spartans will face North Carolina on Monday night after the Tar Heels overwhelmed Villanova 83-69 in the second national semifinal. The matchup gives Michigan State a chance to win a championship less than 100 miles from its East Lansing campus—and to avenge a 98-63 loss to North Carolina at Ford Field in December.

Kalin Lucas scored 21 points and Raymar Morgan added 18 as Michigan State broke open a tight game with defense, depth and a relentless transition attack. The Spartans trailed Connecticut 36-33 at halftime but seized control after the break, forcing turnovers and repeatedly racing past the Huskies for fast-break opportunities.

Michigan State’s bench played a major role, helping the Spartans maintain their pace against a Connecticut team built around 7-foot-3 center Hasheem Thabeet. Rather than allowing the Huskies to settle into their half-court offense, Michigan State pressured the ball and turned defensive stops into momentum-changing baskets.

A second-half sequence captured the shift. The Spartans forced a turnover, pushed the ball downcourt and finished in transition, bringing the largely pro-Michigan State crowd to its feet. Moments later, another Connecticut mistake led to another quick score. What had been a physical, even contest began to tilt decisively toward the Spartans.

Thabeet finished with 17 points for Connecticut, while Stanley Robinson and A.J. Price also reached double figures. But the Huskies committed 16 turnovers, and Michigan State converted those mistakes into 23 points.

Coach Tom Izzo’s team also refused to be intimidated inside. Connecticut entered the game with superior size and one of the nation’s best shot blockers in Thabeet, but Michigan State attacked the basket, competed on the glass and used multiple defenders to keep the Huskies from controlling the paint.

For Izzo, the victory continued a remarkable postseason record. Michigan State reached the championship game for the second time under the Hall of Fame coach and moved within one win of its third national title. The Spartans won their previous championships in 1979, behind Magic Johnson, and in 2000, with Izzo leading the program.

North Carolina’s path to Monday’s final was more direct.

The Tar Heels used a barrage of early 3-pointers to take control against Villanova, building a 49-40 halftime lead and never allowing the Wildcats to establish the rhythm that had carried them through the East Regional.

Ty Lawson led North Carolina with 22 points, Wayne Ellington scored 20 and Tyler Hansbrough added 18. The Tar Heels made 11 3-pointers and repeatedly punished Villanova for collapsing its defense toward Hansbrough.

Ellington was especially effective from the perimeter, finding open space as North Carolina moved the ball quickly around the Wildcats’ defense. Lawson controlled the tempo, attacking off the dribble when Villanova extended its pressure and finding shooters when help defenders stepped into the lane.

Villanova, which had beaten Pittsburgh on Scottie Reynolds’ last-second drive in the regional final, could not produce another comeback. The Wildcats struggled from long range, making only five of 27 3-point attempts. Reynolds scored 17 points but went 6-for-18 from the field as North Carolina’s length and depth made clean looks difficult.

The Tar Heels led by double figures for much of the second half. Each time Villanova threatened to narrow the margin, North Carolina answered—sometimes through Lawson’s penetration, sometimes through Hansbrough inside and often through another open perimeter shot.

The victory placed North Carolina in the championship game for the ninth time and gave coach Roy Williams an opportunity to win his second national title with the Tar Heels. North Carolina won the championship under Williams in 2005 and will seek the fifth NCAA title in program history.

Monday’s final will carry an unusual combination of familiarity and uncertainty. North Carolina has already routed Michigan State on the same court this season, but the Spartans who emerged from the tournament’s first five rounds have looked far different from the team that played the Tar Heels in early December.

Michigan State was without a fully healthy lineup in that first meeting and had not yet developed the defensive identity that has powered its March run. The Spartans have since beaten Southern California, Kansas, Louisville and Connecticut, surviving a difficult road to the championship game.

North Carolina, meanwhile, remains the tournament favorite. The Tar Heels possess experience, scoring balance and perhaps the nation’s most dynamic point guard in Lawson. They can play through Hansbrough in the post, stretch defenses with Ellington and Danny Green, and turn rebounds into instant offense.

To win, Michigan State will have to slow that transition game, control the boards and avoid the turnovers that North Carolina converted so easily in December. The Spartans will also need another aggressive performance from Lucas, whose ability to penetrate could test the Tar Heels’ defense.

Beyond the basketball, the Final Four has carried special significance for Detroit.

The city welcomed the event during a period of profound economic strain. The national recession had hit the region hard, and the crisis surrounding the American automobile industry placed Detroit at the center of the country’s financial uncertainty. Layoffs, declining tax revenue and concerns about the future of General Motors and Chrysler formed the backdrop to the tournament.

Against that setting, the Final Four brought a surge of visitors, national television exposure and business to downtown hotels, restaurants and bars. Tens of thousands of fans filled the streets around Ford Field, Comerica Park and the city’s entertainment districts, providing an important boost to businesses dealing with the downturn.

The event also offered Detroit a chance to present a different image to the country. Instead of abandoned factories and economic distress, national audiences saw a packed downtown stadium, crowded public events and a city capable of staging one of American sports’ largest spectacles.

Ford Field’s configuration created a crowd of more than 72,000 for the semifinals, then a record for a Final Four session. The building’s vastness gave college basketball’s showcase the scale of a major civic event, and Michigan State’s presence transformed much of the crowd into a partisan sea of green and white.

For local fans, the Spartans’ run has added an emotional dimension. Michigan State is not merely representing a school; in the eyes of many supporters, it is carrying the hopes of a state battered by job losses and economic uncertainty.

Izzo, a Michigan native who has spent his entire head-coaching career at Michigan State, has acknowledged that connection throughout the tournament. His team cannot solve Detroit’s economic problems, but for one weekend it has given the region a reason to gather, celebrate and believe in a comeback.

Now the Spartans have one game remaining—and the most difficult opponent in college basketball standing between them and a championship.

On Monday night, Michigan State will again take the floor in what amounts to a home arena. North Carolina will bring the star power, the experience and the memory of December’s 35-point victory.

Detroit will bring the noise.

City leaders and local businesses hope the Final Four will fill hotels, restaurants and bars while generating work for security personnel, caterers, transportation providers and event staff. The influx comes as Detroit contends with high unemployment, population loss and the continuing struggles of the auto industry.

The event alone cannot solve those problems, but officials see it as an opportunity to create temporary jobs, attract visitors and challenge negative perceptions of the city. National television coverage will feature Ford Field and the surrounding downtown area, where fans are expected to attend concerts, public practices and other tournament-related events.

Beyond the financial impact, Detroit is looking for something less easily measured: civic pride.

Major sporting events have long provided common ground in a region closely identified with its teams. Organizers hope the Final Four will give residents another reason to gather downtown and demonstrate that the city remains capable of hosting events on the largest stage.

With roughly 70,000 fans expected inside Ford Field and many more taking part in festivities around the city, Detroit’s first Final Four is being viewed as more than a basketball tournament. For one weekend, it is also a chance for the city to present a different image of itself — busy, welcoming and looking toward a comeback.
